title: The four UML relationships
idea: UML relationships say how strongly two classes are tied: dependency uses briefly, association knows, aggregation groups shared parts, composition owns parts that die with it.

analogy.text: A car's chassis is built with the car and scrapped with it. A car park holds cars that leave freely. A borrowed jump-starter is used once, then returned.
analogy.breaks: Java never scraps objects; the garbage collector frees unreferenced ones.

points: Dependency is a dashed arrow: a parameter or local variable, no stored field.
Association is a solid line: a stored reference, both sides live independently.
A hollow diamond marks aggregation: the whole groups parts it does not own.
A filled diamond marks composition: the whole creates its parts; they die together.

steps.caption: Weakest first. `Player` receives a `Track` as a parameter and keeps nothing. That is a dependency: dashed arrow.
`Album` stores a reference to its `Artist`. Neither creates the other, and the artist outlives any album.
`Playlist` holds tracks someone else made. Clearing it leaves every track alive: hollow diamond, aggregation.
`Album` builds its tracks inside `addTrack` and never hands out its list. Filled diamond: composition.
To choose, ask three questions: is it stored, who creates it, and does it die with the whole?

code.title: The problem
code.caption: The diagram says composition, but the code shares its parts. Outsiders rewrite the album.

walk.text: The caller builds the parts and passes its own list. The album never created its tracks.
c02-t05 calls any has-a field composition; UML composition is stricter: the whole creates and owns the part.
The constructor stores that list and the getter returns it: both ends alias the internals.
`Track` is mutable, so any holder of a reference can rename it.
A playlist renames what it thinks is its own track; the album's track changes too.
The caller reuses its list, and the album silently loses every track.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: Each relationship coded to its real strength: owned parts are created and hidden inside the whole.

walk.text: `Track` is an immutable record, so sharing it is safe; the album still controls its own list.
Association: the artist arrives from outside and is stored, but never created or destroyed here.
Composition: `addTrack` creates each part, so no outsider holds the album's list.
The getter returns a copy; `List.copyOf` is unmodifiable, so callers cannot edit the parts.
Aggregation: the playlist stores tracks made elsewhere, and clearing it destroys nothing.
Dependency: `Player` uses a `Track` only during the call, with no field.
Clearing the playlist leaves the album whole, and outside edits are rejected.

code.title: The diagram
code.caption: The fixed design in Mermaid: `*--` composition, `o--` aggregation, `-->` association, `..>` dependency.

pitfalls: Calling every collection field aggregation; interviewers then ask who creates the parts and you stall.
Composing parts the caller builds or can still change; the whole no longer controls them.
Drawing a field arrow for a parameter-only use exaggerates coupling; use a dashed dependency.

quiz.q: An `Order` builds its `OrderLine` objects internally; they are deleted with it. Which relationship?
options: Aggregation, because an order holds many lines
Dependency, because lines are created in a method
Composition, because lines live and die with the order
Association, because the order stores references
quiz.why: The whole creates the parts, nobody else owns them, and they end with it. Holding many is not enough for aggregation; lifetime ownership decides.

takeaway: Stored? Created by whom? Dies with the whole? That picks the line.

starters: Is aggregation still worth drawing, or is association enough?
Can a composed part be passed to another object temporarily?
How do these relationships map to JPA cascade settings?
